title: Workflow for retrieving data analysis in Medicine and Social Sciences journals
author: Erika EAS Alves dos Santos
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.bbifikbn
materials: The recommended reference management softwares: There are plenty of reference management softwares available to the scientific community, some made available free of charge, some not. Some publishers recommend the use of these tools, some do not. In order to identify the level of the editorial appeal regarding the use of these instruments, the analysis should consider whether the publishers recommend the use of these tools or not. For the cases in which publishers make available a specific plugin for any reference style management software, or even mention a specific software, the analysis should consider a reference management recommendation.

steps.title: Retrieve Journal Titles from SCImago
steps.instruction: Conduct a search in the SCImago database to retrieve journal titles based on specific delimitation parameters.

substeps.instruction: Navigate to the SCImago database homepage (https://www.scimagojr.com/) and click the 'Journal Rankings' hyperlink.
Select the subject area of interest in the 'All subject areas' selection box (keep 'all subject categories' as default).
Select the country or countries of interest, or leave 'All regions/country' as default.
Select 'journals' in the 'All types' selection box.
Select the desired year of publication.
Optional: Check 'only open access journal' to restrict to open access records.
Optional: Check 'Only Scielo Journals' to restrict to SciELO indexed journals.
Optional: Check 'Only WoS Journals' to restrict to Web of Science indexed journals.
Optional: In the 'display journals with at last ____' field, enter a numeric value and select either 'citable docs. (3 years)' or 'total cites (3 years)' to delimit results.
Click the 'apply' button to execute the search.
Optional: Click 'download data' to export results to an Excel sheet.

steps.title: Calculate Subject Area Representativeness
steps.instruction: Determine the proportional representativeness of each subject area to establish the sample size.

substeps.instruction: Repeat the search process for every subject area of interest.
Record the total number of journals indexed for each specific subject area.
Divide the total number of journals in a specific subject area by the total amount of journals indexed in the SCImago database as a whole.
Multiply the result by 100 to get the percentual index of representativeness.
Calculate the number of journals to be selected for the sample based on this percentage, rounding according to mathematical principles.
Ensure a minimum of 2 journals are selected for each subject area, regardless of the percentage.

steps.title: Select Journals for Sampling
steps.instruction: Select the specific journal titles for the sample based on ranking and diversity criteria.

substeps.instruction: Identify journals occupying the highest positions in the 'total cites' ranking for the subject area.
Apply the Publisher Criterion: Do not select more than one journal from the same publisher within the same subject area.
Apply the Subject Category Criterion: Select only journals classified under a single subject area and a single subject category to avoid overlaps.
If a top-ranked journal fails these criteria, replace it with the immediately subsequent journal in the 'total cites' ranking until the target sample size is reached.

steps.title: Define Chronological Coverage
steps.instruction: Establish a chronological parameter (e.g., a specific month, semester, or year) for the sample to align with the study scope.

substeps.instruction: Choose a relatively short interval (e.g., one month) to ensure data is manageable but sufficient.

steps.title: Select Articles from Journal Issues
steps.instruction: Select 5 articles per journal issue using a random exponential method based on the average number of articles (X) published by the selected journals in the defined period.

substeps.instruction: Identify the positions of the 5 articles to be selected: Xth, 2Xth, 3Xth, 4Xth, and 5Xth.

If an issue has fewer than X articles, use a cycle counting process: count from the first article to the last, then return to the first and continue until 5 articles are selected, resetting the count to the article immediately following each selection and disregarding already selected articles.

Include only original research communications (synonyms: articles, papers, researches, original papers, original articles, original researches, research papers, research articles, regular papers, regular articles, regular researches).
If an issue contains no original communications, replace it with the immediately previous eligible issue of the same journal.

Ensure the article has a bibliographic references section (exclusive list or footnotes in Vancouver, Chicago, or APA style). Discard journals where references are mixed with text notes unless clearly differentiable.
For journals with multidisciplinary summaries, count only the first appearance of an article title; exclude duplicates.
Exclude articles not assigned to an issue, unless the publisher does not use issue numbers (in which case, treat the previous period as a virtual regular issue).
Exclude non-regular issues (supplements, special, thematic, or commemorative issues) and replace them with the immediately previous eligible issue.
Prioritize PDF versions; use HTML or hardcopy if PDF is unavailable. If no access is possible, replace the journal with the next eligible one.

steps.title: Perform Journal-Level Analysis
steps.instruction: Analyze general aspects of the journals and their author instructions using a quantitative approach (converting results to numbers or percentages).

substeps.instruction: Verify modality of access: classify as freely available (unrestricted online access), restricted access (payment required), or mixed access (treated as not freely available). Note the browser, version, and IP nationality used.
Identify the reference style adopted via the 'instructions for authors' on the publisher's webpage.
Check for customizations of standard styles (Vancouver, Chicago, AMA, APA), specifically regarding author counts in pointers and references.
Evaluate the maximum number of bibliographic references allowed per article.
Assess the clarity of publishing instructions: classify as 'clear' (comprehensive or refers to a standard style) or 'unclear' (lacks detail on specific publication types like theses).
Analyze the titles used for the bibliographic reference sessions.
Identify the reference assortment: citation-sequence (numerical) or author-date.
Evaluate the provision of citation metadata export tools (machine-readable vs. human-readable) and calculate the percentage of journals providing them.
Check for the presence of basic bibliographic metadata (journal title, year, volume, issue, pages) in headers or footers (Yes/No).

steps.title: Perform Article-Level Analysis
steps.instruction: Conduct an in-depth quantitative analysis of the selected articles.

substeps.instruction: Verify the modality of access for each article (freely available vs. restricted), prioritizing the publisher's website over databases like PubMed Central.
Quantify the file format (PDF, HTML, or both).
Analyze the presentation of journal titles in references (full vs. abridged) and identify the abbreviation source.
Count the total number of authors per article.
Calculate the percentage of articles that provide sources for non-textual content (graphics, photos, figures).
Evaluate in-text reference pointers for clarity, correspondence to the bibliographic list, and alignment with FRBR concepts (Work, Expression, Manifestation, Item).
Check if in-text pointers are hyperlinked to references and if the links are 'round' (bidirectional).
Quantify the total number of mentions (interpretative) and quotations (literal) per article.
Count mentions that include pagination data.
Analyze quotations for: (a) presence of initial/final page numbers in pointers, and (b) use of quotation marks or indents. Quotations without proper markup are treated as mentions with pagination.
Quantify the presentation form of quotations (quotation marks vs. indents).
Calculate the average number of mentions/quotations per cited work, author, publication type, and subject area.
Quantify the FRBR relation: determine if pointers refer to Works, Expressions, or Manifestations and compare this to the bibliographic reference level.
Count the total number of bibliographic references per article and compare it to the number of works cited in the text.
Evaluate the use of 'et al.' in pointers and references according to the adopted style guidelines.
Identify unconformities: mentions/quotations without a corresponding reference, or references without a corresponding in-text pointer.
Categorize the types of publications cited (articles, books, proceedings, etc.). Books are counted as printed unless electronic consult is explicitly noted.
Classify the modality of access of cited works (free vs. restricted); hardcopies and books without electronic notes are restricted.
Quantify the presence of DOI numbers and hypertext links in references for freely available works.
Test all hypertext and DOI links for 'link rot' (broken links) or redirection to non-original pages (e.g., catalogs).
Observe the format of reference numbers for citation-sequence systems.
Compile a metadata set for each reference, marking descriptive elements as 'included' or 'not included' to define an 'essential metadata set'.
Verify the correctness of the reference list assortment (alphabetical for author-date, numerical for citation-sequence).
